fig.caption: The standard normal: z counts standard deviations from the mean. Negative z is below the mean.

steps.title: \(z\) counts standard deviations
steps.body:
\(z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\) is in the formula booklet.
•  \(z\) has no units: it counts standard deviations from the mean
•  a negative \(z\) means the value is below the mean
•  the probability does not change when you standardise: \(\mathrm{P}(X<x)=\mathrm{P}(Z<z)\), where \(Z \sim \mathrm{N}(0,\,1)\)

steps.title: Anna scored \(80\) on her test and Ben scored \(65\) on his. Who did better relative to their class?
steps.ok: ✓ Right. Anna is \(2\) standard deviations above her mean, \(\frac{80-70}{5}=2\); Ben is \(\frac{65-60}{4}=1.25\) above his. Compare \(z\), not raw scores or differences.
steps.bad: ✗ Not quite. Anna: \(z=\frac{80-70}{5}=2\). Ben: \(z=\frac{65-60}{4}=1.25\). Anna is further above her mean, so she did better relative to her class.

fig.caption: σ is known, μ is not. The 10% tail fixes how many σ the value 25 sits above μ: z = 1.2816.

steps.title: One unknown
steps.body:
If \(\sigma\) is known and a probability is given, the calculator cannot find \(\mu\) directly:
•  turn the probability into \(z\) with Inverse Normal \((0,\,1)\)
•  write \(\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}=z\)
•  solve for \(\mu\), keeping \(z\) to at least 4 figures

steps.givenNote: call lengths, in minutes; 10% of calls exceed 25 minutes
steps.title: Put the working in order.
steps.ok: ✓ Right. Probability statement, \(z\), equation, solve. That order is also the order of the marks.
steps.bad: ✗ Not quite. Probability statement first (b), then the \(z\) it gives (c), then the equation in \(\mu\) (d), then solve (a).

steps.givenNote: call lengths, in minutes; 10% of calls exceed 25 minutes
steps.title: Find \(\mu\).
instr: Rearrange the equation for \(\mu\), using the stored \(z\).
Type the value to 3 significant figures.
steps.label: \(\mu=\)
steps.ok: ✓ \(19.9\). The mean is below \(25\), as it must be when only \(10\%\) of calls exceed \(25\).
wrongs: \(30.1\) comes from \(z=-1.28\). Only \(10\%\) exceed \(25\), so \(25\) is above the mean and \(z\) is positive: \(\mu\) must be less than \(25\).
\(19.8\) comes from rounding \(z\) to \(1.3\). Keep \(z=1.2816\).
\(19.88\) comes from \(z=1.28\). Rounded \(z\) drifts the answer; keep 4 figures.

steps.title: A student writes “\(z=1.28\), so \(\mu=25-1.28\times4=19.88\)”. Full marks?
opts: Probably not: \(z\) rounded to 3 s.f. gives \(19.88\), outside the tolerance in some schemes
steps.ok: ✓ Right. The method is sound, so the method mark is safe; the accuracy mark is the risk. \(z=1.28\) is only 3 significant figures, and multiplying it by \(4\) turns a small rounding into \(19.88\), while the scheme expects \(19.87\). The next note shows how to keep \(z\) exact on your calculator.
steps.bad: ✗ Not quite. The method is right, so it is not “wrong”, but it is not safely full marks either: \(z\) was rounded to \(1.28\) before being used, and \(25-1.28\times4=19.88\) where the scheme has \(19.87\). Rounding an intermediate value early is an accuracy slip. The next note shows how to keep \(z\) exact.

steps.title: Keep \(z\) exact: store it, don’t retype it
steps.body:
The calculator gives \(z=1.281551\ldots\). Every digit you drop before using it moves the final answer:

• \(z=1.3\) (2 s.f.) gives \(\mu=25-1.3\times4=19.8\)
• \(z=1.28\) (3 s.f.) gives \(19.88\)
• \(z=1.282\) (4 s.f.) gives \(19.87\)
• stored \(z\) gives \(19.874\), so \(19.9\)

Two habits keep the accuracy mark. On paper, write \(z\) to at least 4 significant figures (\(z=1.282\)) so the examiner sees an unrounded value. On the calculator, store \(z\) in a variable and use the variable in the next line, so no rounding happens at all. Round once, at the end, to 3 s.f.

Press → (the store arrow key, above AC), then ALPHA and Z, then EXE. Z now holds the full value.
Type 25 − Z × 4 and press EXE: 19.87379. ALPHA Z recalls it.
Tip: Ans → Z works too if the value is already on screen: type Ans, press →, ALPHA Z, EXE.

steps.givenNote: masses, in grams; 5% of items are under 100 g
parts: Which probability statement matches the words?
✓ \(z=-1.6449\): negative, since \(100\) is below the mean.
steps.title: Find \(\sigma\).
instr: Write the probability statement, then find \(z\) for area \(0.05\).
Solve \(\dfrac{100-120}{\sigma}=z\).
Type the value to 3 significant figures.
steps.label: \(\sigma=\)
steps.ok: ✓ \(12.2\). Both sides are negative, so \(\sigma\) comes out positive, as it must.
wrongs: \(-12.2\): a standard deviation cannot be negative. \(100-120=-20\) and \(z=-1.6449\) are both negative, so \(\sigma=+12.2\).
\(20\) is \(120-100\), not yet divided by \(z\).
\(12.16\) is right but 4 s.f.: give \(12.2\).

fig.caption: Two probabilities, two z-values, two equations: enough to find both μ and σ.

steps.title: Both unknown
steps.body:
Two probabilities give two equations:
•  \(\dfrac{x_1-\mu}{\sigma}=z_1\)
•  \(\dfrac{x_2-\mu}{\sigma}=z_2\)

Then either:
•  subtract to get \(\sigma=\dfrac{x_2-x_1}{z_2-z_1}\), then \(\mu\)
•  or type both into the GDC’s simultaneous solver with \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) as the unknowns

Either way, write both equations.
steps.code:
Loaves: \(15\%\) under \(480\) g, \(5\%\) over \(530\) g
\(\mathrm{P}(X<480)=0.15 \Rightarrow z_1=-1.0364\)
\(\mathrm{P}(X<530)=0.95 \Rightarrow z_2=1.6449\)
Multiply \(\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}=z\) through by \(\sigma\) and label the equations:
\[\begin{array}{rrcl}(1)\quad & 480-\mu &=& -1.0364\sigma \\ (2)\quad & 530-\mu &=& 1.6449\sigma \\ \hline (2)-(1):\quad & 50 &=& 2.6813\sigma \end{array}\]
The \(\mu\) terms cancel in the subtraction; \(1.6449-(-1.0364)=2.6813\).

steps.givenNote: masses of loaves, in grams; 15% under 480 g, 5% over 530 g
steps.title: Which pair of \(z\)-values is right?
steps.ok: ✓ Right. \(480\) g has only \(15\%\) below it, so it is below the mean: \(z_1<0\). \(530\) g has \(95\%\) below it: \(z_2=1.645\).
steps.bad: ✗ Not quite. \(480\) is below the mean (\(15\%\) below it), so \(z_1=-1.036\). \(530\) has \(95\%\) below it (\(5\%\) over), so \(z_2=+1.645\). The areas themselves are not \(z\)-values.

parts: The two equations, labelled: \[\begin{array}{rrcl}(1)\quad & 480-\mu &=& -1.0364\sigma \\ (2)\quad & 530-\mu &=& 1.6449\sigma \end{array}\] Which operation eliminates \(\mu\)?

✓ Both equations contain \(-\mu\), so subtracting one from the other removes it: \[\begin{array}{rrcl}(1)\quad & 480-\mu &=& -1.0364\sigma \\ (2)\quad & 530-\mu &=& 1.6449\sigma \\ \hline (2)-(1):\quad & 50 &=& 2.6813\sigma \end{array}\]

✗ Adding keeps \(\mu\) (as \(-2\mu\)); dividing mixes everything. Both equations contain \(-\mu\), so subtract: \[\begin{array}{rrcl}(1)\quad & 480-\mu &=& -1.0364\sigma \\ (2)\quad & 530-\mu &=& 1.6449\sigma \\ \hline (2)-(1):\quad & 50 &=& 2.6813\sigma \end{array}\]
steps.title: Find \(\sigma\) for the loaves.
instr: Subtract the first equation from the second: \(\mu\) cancels.
Or enter both in the simultaneous solver with unknowns \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\).
Type the value to 3 significant figures.
steps.label: \(\sigma=\)
steps.worked:
From the two probabilities: \(z_1=-1.0364\), \(z_2=1.6449\). Label the equations and subtract:
\[\begin{array}{rrcl}(1)\quad & 480-\mu &=& -1.0364\sigma \\ (2)\quad & 530-\mu &=& 1.6449\sigma \\ \hline (2)-(1):\quad & 50 &=& 2.6813\sigma \end{array}\]
The \(\mu\) terms cancel. \(\sigma=\dfrac{50}{2.6813}=18.6\) g
wrongs: \(18.7\) comes from \(z\)-values rounded to 2 d.p. Keep 4 figures: \(18.6\).
\(82.1\) comes from \(z_1=+1.036\). \(480\) is below the mean, so \(z_1\) is negative and the two \(z\)-values are \(2.68\) apart, not \(0.61\).

steps.givenNote: loaves, continuing from the previous step
carry: \(\sigma=18.65\) g (previous step; use your stored value)
parts: ✗ \(480-\mu=-1.0364\sigma\) gives \(\mu=480+1.0364\sigma\); the other equation gives \(\mu=530-1.6449\sigma\), the same value.
steps.title: Find \(\mu\) for the loaves.
instr: Substitute \(\sigma\) into either equation and solve for \(\mu\).
Type the value to 3 significant figures.
steps.label: \(\mu=\)
steps.worked:
Take the first equation: \(480-\mu=-1.0364\sigma\)
\(\mu=480+1.0364\times18.648=499.3\), so \(\mu=499\) g
Check with the second: \(530-1.6449\times18.648=499.3\) ✓ (both equations must agree)
steps.ok: ✓ \(499\). Both equations give the same \(\mu\): a free check.
wrongs: \(461\) comes from \(480-1.036\sigma\): the sign of \(z_1\) is negative, so \(\mu=480+1.036\sigma\).

steps.title: Which working earns full method marks for \(\sigma\) and \(\mu\)?
steps.ok: ✓ Right. Both equations, the \(z\)-values to 4 figures, the method of solving, the answers.
bads: ✗ No equations: examiners note that guess-and-check on the GDC is not valid working here.
✗ \(z\) rounded to 3 s.f. drifts \(\sigma\) to \(18.7\), and the equations are missing.

Then Normal Cdf with the full value of \(\sigma\).

wrongs: \(0.663\) is \(\mathrm{P}(X<26)\), the other tail.

steps.title: “Using \(z\)-values, show that \(\mathrm{P}(284<X<295)\approx0.726\).” Which answer earns the marks?
steps.ok: ✓ Right. “Using \(z\)-values” means the \(z\)-values and the standard-normal probabilities are the working.
steps.bad: ✗ Not quite. The question says using \(z\)-values: \(z=\frac{284-290}{5}=-1.2\) and \(z=\frac{295-290}{5}=1\), then \(\mathrm{P}(-1.2<Z<1)=0.8413-0.1151=0.726\). The GDC value alone scores nothing here.

steps.givenNote: temperatures in °C; \(Y=1.8X+32\) converts to °F. SL students may skip this step
steps.title: If \(Y=aX+b\) then \(\mathrm{E}(Y)=a\,\mathrm{E}(X)+b\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(Y)=a^2\,\mathrm{Var}(X)\), and \(Y\) is still normal. Find \(\mathrm{Var}(Y)\).
steps.ok: ✓ Right. \(\mathrm{Var}(Y)=1.8^2\times4=12.96\), so \(\sigma_Y=3.6\). The \(+32\) moves the mean to \(68\) but not the spread.
steps.bad: ✗ Not quite. \(\mathrm{Var}(Y)=a^2\,\mathrm{Var}(X)=1.8^2\times2^2=12.96\). \(3.6\) is \(\sigma_Y\); \(7.2\) forgets to square \(a\); the \(+32\) affects only the mean.

sets.q: Find the \(z\)-value of a bolt of length \(3.9\) cm.
sets.label: \(z=\)

\(z=1.75\). Check: \(3.9\) is above the mean, so \(z\) is positive; \(0.7\) alone is the gap in cm, not in standard deviations.

parts: Which probability statement, with a LEFT area, matches the words?
✓ “\(20\%\) of times are under \(70\)” is a left area of \(0.2\) already.
✗ “Under \(70\)” means less than \(70\): \(\mathrm{P}(X<70)=0.2\), a left area, no conversion needed.
Which calculator function turns that area into \(z\)?
Inverse Normal with Area = that left area, \(\mu=0\), \(\sigma=1\)
Normal Cdf with the given \(x\) as the upper bound
Inverse Normal with the given \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) of \(X\)
✓ Inverse Normal on the standard normal gives \(z\) directly.

Find \(z\) (keep 4 figures; type at least 3 decimal places).
\(+0.8416\): the area \(0.2\) is less than \(0.5\), so \(70\) is below the mean and \(z\) is negative.
\(0.2\) is the area, not \(z\). Use Inverse Normal with \(\mu=0\), \(\sigma=1\).
